claim: Lysine acetylation is a post-translational modification that is conserved from bacteria to humans.
source: Lysine acetylation is a post-translational modification that is conserved from bacteria to humans.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the conservation of lysine acetylation across domains of life.

claim: Lysine acetylation is catalysed by lysine acetyltransferases, which use acetyl-CoA as the acetyl-donor molecule.
source: It is catalysed by the activities of lysine acetyltransferases, which use acetyl-CoA as the acetyl-donor molecule, and lysine deacetylases, which remove the acetyl moiety.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the enzymatic mechanism of lysine acetylation.

claim: Lysine deacetylases remove the acetyl moiety from acetylated lysines.
source: It is catalysed by the activities of lysine acetyltransferases, which use acetyl-CoA as the acetyl-donor molecule, and lysine deacetylases, which remove the acetyl moiety.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the function of lysine deacetylases.

claim: Tu et al. (2015) reported that YcgC represents a new prokaryotic deacetylase family with no apparent homologies to existing deacetylases.
source: Recently, it was reported that YcgC represents a new prokaryotic deacetylase family with no apparent homologies to existing deacetylases (Tu et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tu et al., 2015.

claim: YcgC is not a deacetylase.
source: Here we report the results of experiments which demonstrate that YcgC is not a deacetylase.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including immunoblotting and mass spectrometry results showing no deacetylase activity.

claim: Quantitative mass spectrometry in the last decade enabled the identification of thousands of lysine acetylation sites in all kingdoms of life.
source: The progress in quantitative mass spectrometry in the last decade enabled the identification of thousands of lysine acetylation sites in all kingdoms of life (Choudhary et al., 2009; Lundby et al., 2012; Weinert et al., 2014, 2017, 2013b; Zhang et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: Histones were known since the 1960s to be modified by lysine acetylation.
source: While histones were known since the 1960 s to be modified by lysine acetylation, these studies revealed that proteins of all cellular compartments covering essential cellular functions are lysine acetylated in eukaryotes, archaea and prokaryotes (Finkemeier et al., 2011; König et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established historical scientific knowledge.

claim: Proteins of all cellular compartments covering essential cellular functions are lysine acetylated in eukaryotes, archaea and prokaryotes.
source: While histones were known since the 1960 s to be modified by lysine acetylation, these studies revealed that proteins of all cellular compartments covering essential cellular functions are lysine acetylated in eukaryotes, archaea and prokaryotes (Finkemeier et al., 2011; König et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Lysine acetylation is a dynamic post-translational modification catalysed by lysine acetyltransferases and lysine deacetylases.
source: Lysine acetylation is a dynamic post-translational modification that is catalysed by lysine acetyltransferases, which add the acetyl moiety and lysine deacetylases (KDACs) which remove it.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the dynamic nature of lysine acetylation.

claim: Site-specific non-enzymatic acetylation has been reported.
source: Site-specific non-enzymatic acetylation has also been reported (Baeza et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Baeza et al., 2015.

claim: Two classes of deacetylases exist in eukaryotes: the classical Zn2+-dependent KDACs and the NAD+-dependent sirtuins.
source: While two classes of deacetylases exist in eukaryotes, the classical Zn2+-dependent KDACs and the NAD+-dependent sirtuins, prokaryotes only encode for sirtuins.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about deacetylase classes in eukaryotes.

claim: Prokaryotes only encode for sirtuins.
source: While two classes of deacetylases exist in eukaryotes, the classical Zn2+-dependent KDACs and the NAD+-dependent sirtuins, prokaryotes only encode for sirtuins.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about deacetylases in prokaryotes.

claim: Escherichia coli encodes for only one single KDAC, the sirtuin deacetylase CobB.
source: Escherichia coli encodes for only one single KDAC, the sirtuin deacetylase CobB, which is structurally highly similar to eukaryotic sirtuins showing only minor structural differences in the small Zn2+-binding domain (Zhao et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Zhao et al., 2004.

claim: CobB is structurally highly similar to eukaryotic sirtuins showing only minor structural differences in the small Zn2+-binding domain.
source: Escherichia coli encodes for only one single KDAC, the sirtuin deacetylase CobB, which is structurally highly similar to eukaryotic sirtuins showing only minor structural differences in the small Zn2+-binding domain (Zhao et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Zhao et al., 2004.

claim: In mammals there are seven sirtuin deacylases (Sirt1-7), which show distinct subcellular localisation.
source: In contrast, in mammals there are seven sirtuin deacylases (Sirt1-7), which show distinct subcellular localisation.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about mammalian sirtuins.

claim: The nuclear Sirt1, the cytosolic Sirt2 and the mitochondrial Sirt3 possess a robust deacetylase activity.
source: While the nuclear Sirt1, the cytosolic Sirt2 and the mitochondrial Sirt3 possess a robust deacetylase activity, the remaining deacetylases show preferences for longer acylations or act as ADP-ribosyltransferases (Du et al., 2011; Feldman et al., 2013; Liszt et al., 2005; Smith et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: The remaining mammalian sirtuins show preferences for longer acylations or act as ADP-ribosyltransferases.
source: While the nuclear Sirt1, the cytosolic Sirt2 and the mitochondrial Sirt3 possess a robust deacetylase activity, the remaining deacetylases show preferences for longer acylations or act as ADP-ribosyltransferases (Du et al., 2011; Feldman et al., 2013; Liszt et al., 2005; Smith et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: Mammals encode eleven classical KDACs and seven sirtuins.
source: Mammals encode eleven classical KDACs and seven sirtuins enabling to use some activities with rather low specificity, while other enzymes show a remarkable specificity for some substrates and some lysine acylation sites (Knyphausen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Some mammalian deacetylases have low specificity, while other enzymes show remarkable specificity for some substrates and some lysine acylation sites.
source: Mammals encode eleven classical KDACs and seven sirtuins enabling to use some activities with rather low specificity, while other enzymes show a remarkable specificity for some substrates and some lysine acylation sites (Knyphausen et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Knyphausen et al., 2016.

claim: Mammals use post-translational lysine acylation as a molecular switch with consequences on signal transduction and regulation of protein function.
source: This allows mammals to use post-translational lysine acylation as a molecular switch with consequences on signal transduction and regulation of protein function.
evidence: This is an inference based on the diversity and specificity of mammalian deacetylases.

claim: The prokaryotic CobB has a broad substrate range and is quite promiscuous with respect to its substrate proteins.
source: In contrast, the prokaryotic CobB has a broad substrate range and it is quite promiscuous with respect to its substrate proteins.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about CobB substrate specificity.

claim: CobB's major role is the detoxification of lysine acylations occurring upon metabolic fuel switching or metabolic stress under conditions of accumulation of acetyl-CoA or acetyl-phosphate.
source: This suggests CobB's major role to be the detoxification of lysine acylations occuring upon metabolic fuel switching or metabolic stress under conditions of accumulation of acetyl-CoA or acetyl-phosphate, which can both serve as acetyl group donor molecules in prokaryotes (Weinert et al., 2013a, 2017).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Acetyl-CoA and acetyl-phosphate can both serve as acetyl group donor molecules in prokaryotes.
source: This suggests CobB's major role to be the detoxification of lysine acylations occuring upon metabolic fuel switching or metabolic stress under conditions of accumulation of acetyl-CoA or acetyl-phosphate, which can both serve as acetyl group donor molecules in prokaryotes (Weinert et al., 2013a, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Weinert et al., 2013a, 2017.

claim: YcgC (also termed DhaM) together with YcgT (DhaK) and YcgS (DhaL) was originally reported to be part of the active dihydroxyacetone kinase (DhaK) complex.
source: YcgC (also termed DhaM) together with YcgT (DhaK) and YcgS (DhaL) was originally reported to be part of the active dihydroxyacetone kinase (DhaK) complex.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about YcgC's original characterization.

claim: YcgC is a component of a phosphorelay system using phosphoenolpyruvate as phosphoryl donor in which the phosphoryl group is finally transferred by DhaK to dihydroxyacetone yielding dihydroxyacetone phosphate.
source: It is a component of a phosphorelay system using phosphoenolpyruvate as phosphoryl donor in which the phosphoryl group is finally transferred by DhaK to dihydroxyacetone yielding dihydroxyacetone phosphate (Gutknecht et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gutknecht et al., 2001.

claim: YcgC has no sequence or structural homology to either eukaryotic classical KDACs or to sirtuin deacylases.
source: YcgC has no sequence or structural homology to either eukaryotic classical KDACs or to sirtuin deacylases and it does not depend on Zn2+ or NAD+ for catalysis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about YcgC structure.

claim: YcgC does not depend on Zn2+ or NAD+ for catalysis.
source: YcgC has no sequence or structural homology to either eukaryotic classical KDACs or to sirtuin deacylases and it does not depend on Zn2+ or NAD+ for catalysis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about YcgC's catalytic mechanism.

claim: Tu et al. reported that YcgC acts as serine hydrolase using a distinct catalytic mechanism involving a catalytic serine residue (S200).
source: Tu et al. reported that YcgC acts as serine hydrolase using a distinct catalytic mechanism involving a catalytic serine residue (S200); they also reported that YcgC catalyses deacetylation of the transcriptional regulator RutR and supports subsequent autoproteolytic cleavage at the RutR N-terminus (Tu et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tu et al., 2015.

claim: Tu et al. reported that YcgC catalyses deacetylation of the transcriptional regulator RutR and supports subsequent autoproteolytic cleavage at the RutR N-terminus.
source: Tu et al. reported that YcgC acts as serine hydrolase using a distinct catalytic mechanism involving a catalytic serine residue (S200); they also reported that YcgC catalyses deacetylation of the transcriptional regulator RutR and supports subsequent autoproteolytic cleavage at the RutR N-terminus (Tu et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tu et al., 2015.

claim: The authors were unable to detect any deacetylase activity of YcgC.
source: In summary, we were unable to detect any deacetylase activity of YcgC, which means that CobB would seem to be the only deacetylase present in E. coli, and that YcgC should not be annotated as a lysine deacetylase in UniProt and other databases.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: CobB is the only deacetylase present in E. coli.
source: In summary, we were unable to detect any deacetylase activity of YcgC, which means that CobB would seem to be the only deacetylase present in E. coli, and that YcgC should not be annotated as a lysine deacetylase in UniProt and other databases.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of YcgC deacetylase activity and established knowledge about E. coli deacetylases.

claim: YcgC should not be annotated as a lysine deacetylase in UniProt and other databases.
source: In summary, we were unable to detect any deacetylase activity of YcgC, which means that CobB would seem to be the only deacetylase present in E. coli, and that YcgC should not be annotated as a lysine deacetylase in UniProt and other databases.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing no deacetylase activity.

claim: YcgC, YcgC S200A, CobB and CobB H110Y were recombinantly expressed in E. coli BL21 (DE3) cells and purified to a high level of purity.
source: We recombinantly expressed YcgC, the supposed deacetylase-dead mutant YcgC S200A, CobB and the catalytically inactive mutant CobB H110Y in E. coli BL21 (DE3) cells and purified them to a high level of purity using a two-step purification strategy composed of a glutathione (GSH)-affinity purification step followed by size exclusion-chromatography (SEC).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data describing the protein purification methods.

claim: All proteins could be successfully produced and showed final purities of more than 95%.
source: All proteins could be successfully produced and showed final purities of more than 95% (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: YcgC and the mutant YcgC S200A behaved similar on analytical SEC.
source: YcgC and the mutant YcgC S200A behaved similar on analytical SEC further underlining the high quality of proteins (Figure 1B, upper panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Tu et al. reported that YcgC deacetylates the transcriptional regulator RutR acetylated at K52 (RutR AcK52) and at K62 (RutR AcK62).
source: Tu et al. reported that YcgC deacetylates the transcriptional regulator RutR acetylated at K52 (RutR AcK52) and at K62 (RutR AcK62).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tu et al.

claim: An E. coli BL21 (DE3) strain carrying a genomic deletion of ycgC and cobB was constructed to exclude the possibility that RutR is deacetylated endogenously during expression.
source: For expression of acetylated RutR, we constructed an E. coli BL21 (DE3) strain carrying a genomic deletion of ycgC and cobB (E. coli BL21 (DE3) ΔycgCΔcobB) to exclude the possibility that RutR is deacetylated endogenously during the expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data describing the strain construction.

claim: The genetic code expansion concept was used to site-specifically introduce acetyl-L-lysine at positions K52 and K62 into RutR.
source: We used the genetic code expansion concept to site-specifically introduce acetyl-L-lysine at positions K52 and K62 into RutR.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data describing the method used.

claim: Non-acetylated RutR wildtype (WT), RutR AcK52 and RutR AcK62 were produced and purified to high degree with sufficient yield to perform biochemical studies.
source: We were able to produce non-acetylated RutR wildtype (WT), RutR AcK52 and RutR AcK62 purified to high degree and obtained a yield sufficient to perform biochemical studies.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data describing protein production.

claim: Immunoblotting, electrospray ionisation mass spectrometry (ESI-MS) and tryptic digest followed by UPLC-MS/MS confirmed that RutR is quantitatively, homogenously and site-specifically lysine acetylated at positions K52 and K62.
source: Immunoblotting, electrospray ionisation mass spectrometry (ESI-MS) as well as tryptic digest and subsequent ultra-performance liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry (UPLC-MS/MS) confirmed that RutR is quantitatively, homogenously and site-specifically lysine acetylated at the positions K52 and K62 (Figure 1C,D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in multiple figures.

claim: RutR WT was not acetylated on Lys upon expression in either E. coli BL21 (DE3) or in E. coli BL21 (DE3) ΔycgCΔcobB.
source: Notably, RutR WT was not acetylated on Lys upon expression in either E. coli BL21 (DE3) or in E. coli BL21 (DE3) ΔycgCΔcobB.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mass spectrometry and immunoblotting.

claim: Tu et al. reported that RutR expressed in E. coli W3110 is almost quantitatively lysine acetylated.
source: This is in contrast to the report by Tu et al., according to which RutR expressed in E. coli W3110 is almost quantitatively lysine acetylated (Figure 1C,D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tu et al.

claim: LC-MS/MS data revealed that the RutR protein from Tu et al. is not quantitatively lysine acetylated.
source: As shown later, our LC-MS/MS data revealed that also the RutR protein from Tu et al. is not quantitatively lysine acetylated.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental LC-MS/MS data presented later in the manuscript.

claim: All RutR proteins eluted not in the exclusion volume, showed a highly symmetric elution peak and eluted at an almost identical elution volume in analytical SEC runs.
source: In analytical SEC runs, all RutR proteins eluted not in the exclusion volume, showed a highly symmetric elution peak and eluted at an almost identical elution volume.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental SEC data.

claim: All RutR proteins are in a similar oligomeric state.
source: This shows that all proteins are in a similar oligomeric state and it furthermore suggests that lysine acetylation of RutR does not interfere with protein folding or the oligomeric state (Figure 1B, lower panel).
evidence: This is an inference based on SEC elution profiles shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Lysine acetylation of RutR does not interfere with protein folding or the oligomeric state.
source: This shows that all proteins are in a similar oligomeric state and it furthermore suggests that lysine acetylation of RutR does not interfere with protein folding or the oligomeric state (Figure 1B, lower panel).
evidence: This is an inference based on SEC elution profiles shown in Figure 1B.

claim: YcgC did not catalyze deacetylation of RutR AcK52 or RutR AcK62.
source: We did not observe any YcgC catalysed deacetylation of RutR AcK52 or RutR AcK62 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: RutR AcK52 was strongly deacetylated by CobB.
source: As shown by immunoblotting, RutR AcK52 was strongly deacetylated by CobB whereas RutR AcK62 was only slightly deacetylated (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: RutR AcK62 was only slightly deacetylated by CobB.
source: As shown by immunoblotting, RutR AcK52 was strongly deacetylated by CobB whereas RutR AcK62 was only slightly deacetylated (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: ESI-MS analysis confirmed that no YcgC deacetylase activity towards either RutR AcK52 or RutR AcK62 was measurable.
source: Again, no YcgC deacetylase activity towards either RutR AcK52 or RutR AcK62 was measurable and only one single peak with a mass of 24608 Da exactly corresponding to mono-lysine acetylated RutR was detectable (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental ESI-MS data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: RutR AcK52 was deacetylated by CobB to more than 60% resulting in a mass shift of 42 Da.
source: In contrast, RutR AcK52 was deacetylated by CobB to more than 60% resulting in a mass shift of 42 Da, which agrees with removal of an acetyl-group, while RutR AcK62 was only marginally deacetylated by CobB (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental ESI-MS data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The mass shift of 42 Da agrees with removal of an acetyl-group.
source: In contrast, RutR AcK52 was deacetylated by CobB to more than 60% resulting in a mass shift of 42 Da, which agrees with removal of an acetyl-group, while RutR AcK62 was only marginally deacetylated by CobB (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge that an acetyl group has a mass of 42 Da.

claim: YcgC does not have any deacetylase activity towards RutR AcK52 and AcK62.
source: These data support the immunoblotting experiments and clearly show that YcgC does not have any deacetylase activity towards RutR AcK52 and AcK62.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from immunoblotting and mass spectrometry.

claim: No (auto-)proteolytic cleavage of RutR WT, RutR AcK52 or RutR AcK62 was observed, independently of presence or absence of YcgC.
source: Moreover, we did not observe any (auto-)proteolytic cleavage of RutR WT, RutR AcK52 or RutR AcK62, independently of presence or absence of YcgC.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from SDS-PAGE, immunoblotting and ESI-MS.

claim: The antibody ab21263 from abcam detected site-specifically lysine-acetylated RutR AcK52 and AcK62, while none of the other proteins were stained.
source: Using the antibody from abcam we confirmed the results obtained before. We only detected site-specifically lysine-acetylated RutR AcK52 and AcK62, while none of the other proteins were stained with the anti-acetyl-lysine antibody from abcam (ab21263) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental immunoblotting data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The antibody CST9441 used by Tu et al. detected all RutR proteins used in this study, including non-acetylated RutR.
source: Notably, the antibody CST9441 used by Tu et al. detected all RutR proteins used in this study, i.e. non-acetylated RutR prepared by our group, RutR AcK52 and AcK62, as well as RutR from Tu et al.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental immunoblotting data.

claim: The antibody from abcam detected a CobB catalysed decrease in acetylation-level for RutR AcK52 (and more weakly also for AcK62).
source: Moreover, while we observed a CobB catalysed decrease in acetylation-level using the antibody from abcam for RutR Ack52 (and more weakly also for AcK62) as expected, the antibody CST9441 did not detect a decrease in acetylation signal intensity upon CobB treatment (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental immunoblotting data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The antibody CST9441 did not detect a decrease in acetylation signal intensity upon CobB treatment.
source: Moreover, while we observed a CobB catalysed decrease in acetylation-level using the antibody from abcam for RutR Ack52 (and more weakly also for AcK62) as expected, the antibody CST9441 did not detect a decrease in acetylation signal intensity upon CobB treatment (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental immunoblotting data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The CST9441 antibody detects trace amounts of acetylation occurring at very low stoichiometry most likely non-enzymatically during expression in E. coli.
source: This suggests that it detects trace amounts of acetylation occurring at very low stoichiometry most likely non-enzymatically during expression in E. coli.
evidence: This is an inference based on the antibody's detection pattern.

claim: The CST9441 antibody shows cross-reactivity with other antigenic components, for example the RutR protein sequence.
source: Alternatively, the CST9441 antibody shows cross-reactivity with other antigenic components, for example the RutR protein sequence.
evidence: This is speculation about an alternative explanation for the antibody's behavior.

claim: The antibody CST9441 might not be suitable for these assays.
source: In both cases, the antibody CST9441 might not be suitable for these assays.
evidence: This is an inference based on the antibody's detection pattern and lack of specificity.

claim: ESI-MS showed no additional lysine acetylations on RutR proteins prepared by the authors.
source: To underline these conclusions, we observed for our RutR proteins no additional lysine acetylations by ESI-MS showing that if further acetylations happen on the RutR protein, these are present at very low, highly sub-stoichiometric levels (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental ESI-MS data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: If further acetylations happen on the RutR protein, these are present at very low, highly sub-stoichiometric levels.
source: To underline these conclusions, we observed for our RutR proteins no additional lysine acetylations by ESI-MS showing that if further acetylations happen on the RutR protein, these are present at very low, highly sub-stoichiometric levels (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is an inference based on ESI-MS data.

claim: Treatment with YcgC prepared by Tu et al. resulted in reduction of molecular size of RutR proteins.
source: We observe a reduction of the molecular size upon treatment with the YcgC prepared by Tu et al., but neither for YcgC prepared by us, nor by YcgC S200A prepared by Tu et al., suggesting that the YcgC preparation from Tu et al. contains an activity explaining this observation (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The YcgC preparation from Tu et al. contains an activity that causes reduction in molecular size of RutR.
source: We observe a reduction of the molecular size upon treatment with the YcgC prepared by Tu et al., but neither for YcgC prepared by us, nor by YcgC S200A prepared by Tu et al., suggesting that the YcgC preparation from Tu et al. contains an activity explaining this observation (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects of different YcgC preparations.

claim: The proteolytic modification of RutR must occur from the N-terminus.
source: This proteolytic modification must occur from the N-terminus as our C-terminally His6-tagged protein still gives a signal in His6 staining, while N-terminally His6-tagged RutR from Tu et al. completely looses His6-staining.
evidence: This is an inference based on His6-tag staining patterns.

claim: For both RutR AcK52 and AcK62 the lower molecular weight RutR protein is still lysine acetylated.
source: Importantly, for both RutR AcK52 and AcK62 the lower molecular weight RutR protein is still lysine acetylated as shown by immunoblotting using the anti-acetyl lysine antibody from abcam suggesting that both proteins are not deacetylated on either AcK52 or AcK62 prior to proteolytic cleavage.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental immunoblotting data.

claim: The autoproteolytic cleavage of RutR is not preceded by the deacetylation of RutR AcK52 and/or AcK62.
source: This clearly shows that the autoproteolytic cleavage of RutR is not preceded by the deacetylation of RutR AcK52 and/or AcK62, as was suggested by Tu et al.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that cleaved RutR is still acetylated.

claim: Non-acetylated RutR can be expressed and purified in full-length without observing truncation at the N-terminus.
source: As additional support, we are able to express and purify non-acetylated RutR in full-length without observing truncation at the N-terminus.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from protein expression and purification.

claim: The YcgC preparation by Tu et al. contained several contaminants that were neither present in the YcgC S200A preparation by Tu et al. nor in the YcgC protein preparation by the authors.
source: We observed, that the YcgC preparation by Tu et al. contained several contaminants that were neither present in the YcgC S200A preparation by Tu et al. nor in our YcgC protein preparation (Supplementary file 1, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS/MS data presented in Supplementary files.

claim: Several proteases and peptidases (metallo- and serine proteases) and several proteins with unknown function were found in the YcgC preparation by Tu et al.
source: Amongst these proteins, we found several proteases and peptidases (metallo- and serine proteases) and several proteins with unknown function (Supplementary file 1, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS/MS data presented in Supplementary files.

claim: Lon protease was detected in YcgC preparation by Tu et al.
source: Notably, we even detected Lon protease in YcgC by Tu et al., which is genomically deleted in most commercially available bacterial expression strains to avoid proteolytic cleavage of expressed proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS/MS data.

claim: Lon protease is genomically deleted in most commercially available bacterial expression strains to avoid proteolytic cleavage of expressed proteins.
source: Notably, we even detected Lon protease in YcgC by Tu et al., which is genomically deleted in most commercially available bacterial expression strains to avoid proteolytic cleavage of expressed proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about bacterial expression strains.

claim: One of Lon protease's best-characterised substrates is the helix-turn-helix (HTH) LuxR-type transcriptional regulator RscA.
source: One of Lon protease's best-characterised substrates is the helix-turn-helix (HTH) LuxR-type transcriptional regulator RscA.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Lon protease substrates.

claim: The HTH TetR-type transcriptional repressor RutR might be a specific substrate of Lon protease.
source: This fuels the idea that maybe the HTH TetR-type transcriptional repressor RutR might be a specific substrate as well. This needs further investigation.
evidence: This is speculation based on structural similarity between RutR and known Lon protease substrates.

claim: The RutR protein from Tu et al. is not quantitatively lysine acetylated.
source: First, the RutR protein is not quantitatively lysine acetylated, as was reported by Tu et al.
evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS/MS data.

claim: The overall amount of acetylated RutR from Tu et al. is 1.09%.
source: In fact, from our mass spectrometrical analyses we can conclude that overall the amount of acetylated RutR is 1.09% (total intensity of 5.74*1011 vs. intensity of acetylated peptides: 6.26*109).
evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS/MS data analysis.

claim: An overall sequence coverage of 90% was obtained in the LC-MS/MS experiments showing that almost all lysines present in RutR are detectable.
source: We obtained an overall sequence coverage of 90% in the LC-MS/MS experiments showing that almost all lysines present in RutR are detectable (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS/MS data presented in Supplementary file 3.

claim: The RutR acetylation is of very low occupancy.
source: Moreover, although we cannot determine precise RutR-acetylation stoichiometries by LC-MS/MS without performing a standard curve, these data clearly show that the RutR acetylation is of very low occupancy.
evidence: This is an inference based on LC-MS/MS intensity data.

claim: Acetylated and non-acetylated peptides show similar ionization efficiencies and MS intensities can be used for quantification of the occupancy.
source: Acetylated and non-acetylated peptides is reported to show similar ionization efficiencies and as a consequence the MS intensities can be used for quantification of the occupancy (Cho et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Cho et al., 2016.

claim: RutR K150 is the acetyl acceptor site with highest occupancy of about 0.7% of total RutR.
source: From the identified acetylated lysines, RutR K150 is the acetyl acceptor site with highest occupancy of about 0.7% of total RutR.
evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS/MS data analysis.

claim: Lysine 21 is the second best acetyl acceptor site with an occupancy of 0.3%.
source: Lysine 21 is the second best acetyl acceptor site with an occupancy of 0.3% followed by AcK95 with 0.06%.
evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS/MS data analysis.

claim: AcK95 has an occupancy of 0.06%.
source: Lysine 21 is the second best acetyl acceptor site with an occupancy of 0.3% followed by AcK95 with 0.06%.
evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS/MS data analysis.

claim: AcK52 was found in the RutR preparation from Tu et al. but in a very low occupancy of only 0.02% in relation to all peptides identified.
source: Second, we found AcK52 in the RutR preparation from Tu et al. but again in a very low occupancy of only 0.02% in relation to all peptides identified.
evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS/MS data analysis.

claim: K62 is not lysine-acetylated at all in the RutR preparation from Tu et al.
source: Third, while Tu and co-workers identified K62 in RutR as the acetylation site of highest functional importance, our LC-MS/MS data revealed that K62 is not lysine-acetylated at all, although this lysine has been identified in the non-acetylated state and in a peptide with one missed cleavage suggesting that the peptide would be analysable by LC-MS/MS if present.
evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS/MS data analysis.

claim: The model presented by Tu et al. needs to be revised.
source: These data clearly show that the model presented by Tu et al. needs to be revised.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data contradicting the Tu et al. model.

claim: YcgC does not show any deacetylase activity towards site-specifically lysine acetylated RutR.
source: In summary, we have shown that YcgC does not show any deacetylase activity towards site-specifically lysine acetylated RutR.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from immunoblotting and mass spectrometry.

claim: YcgC prepared by the authors did neither directly nor indirectly affect RutR proteolytic cleavage or autoproteolysis.
source: Additionally, YcgC prepared in our lab did neither directly nor indirectly affect RutR proteolytic cleavage or autoproteolysis.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from SDS-PAGE and immunoblotting.

claim: RutR from Tu et al. is only marginally lysine-acetylated with an overall occupancy of 1%.
source: LC-MS/MS analyses revealed that RutR from Tu et al. is only marginally lysine-acetylated with an overall occupancy of 1%.
evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS/MS data analysis.

claim: The lower molecular weight RutR proteins produced by treatment with YcgC from Tu et al. were lysine-acetylated.
source: For our site-specifically lysine-acetylated RutR proteins, we also observe proteolytic cleavage by treatment with the YcgC preparation from Tu and co-workers. However, also the lower molecular weight RutR proteins were lysine-acetylated.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental immunoblotting data.

claim: The (auto-)proteolysis of RutR is not preceded by the YcgC-catalysed deacetylation of RutR at AcK52 and/or AcK62.
source: Taken together, these data call into question the molecular model presented by Tu et al.: in other words, the data show that the (auto-)proteolysis of RutR is not preceded by the YcgC-catalysed deacetylation of RutR at AcK52 and/or AcK62.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that cleaved RutR remains acetylated.

claim: LC-MS/MS analyses revealed the presence of a number of contaminants, including some that have proteolytic activity, in the YcgC preparation provided by Tu et al.
source: Our LC-MS/MS analyses revealed the presence of a number of contaminants, including some that have proteolytic activity, in the YcgC preparation provided by Tu et al.
evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS/MS data analysis.

claim: Threading analyses of YcgC using the programme iTASSER revealed no obvious homologies to enzymes with deacetylase or protease activity.
source: Finally, threading analyses of YcgC using the programme iTASSER revealed no obvious homologies to enzymes with deacetylase or protease activity (Supplementary file 4) (Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational analysis using iTASSER.
